clinicalPearls: Lateral elbow pain arising from the common extensor origin, chiefly extensor carpi radialis brevis
Despite the '-itis' name it is a degenerative tendinopathy (angiofibroblastic tendinosis) from overuse, not primary inflammation
Provoked by gripping and wrist and finger extension; pain is reproduced by resisted wrist extension and by Cozen's test
Tenderness is typically just distal and anterior to the lateral epicondyle
Diagnosis is largely clinical, with ultrasound or MRI reserved for uncertain or refractory cases
Often self-limiting; management is load modification, avoiding aggravating grip activity, and progressive or eccentric loading with physiotherapy
Corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with poorer longer-term outcomes and possible tendon harm, so it is used cautiously
Counterforce bracing, and shockwave therapy in resistant cases, may help
reference.pathophysiology: Lateral epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin at the lateral humeral epicondyle, predominantly involving extensor carpi radialis brevis. Repetitive gripping and wrist extension generate cumulative tensile load that exceeds the tendon's repair capacity. Histology shows angiofibroblastic degeneration with disorganised collagen, increased ground substance and neovascularisation, and a notable absence of inflammatory cells, so it is best regarded as a tendinosis rather than a true '-itis'. Chronic change reflects a failed healing response at the enthesis.
additionalDifferentials: Radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve entrapment)
Posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow
Osteochondral or plica pathology of the radiocapitellar joint
additionalInvestigations: Clinical provocative tests (resisted wrist extension, Cozen's test, Mill's test)
Ultrasound to confirm common extensor tendinopathy or a tear
MRI in refractory or diagnostically unclear cases
Plain radiographs to assess the joint and exclude calcification or arthritis
Nerve conduction studies if radial tunnel syndrome or radiculopathy is suspected
redFlags: Neurological symptoms suggesting nerve entrapment or cervical radiculopathy
Night pain, systemic upset or a mass suggesting other pathology
Locking or instability implying intra-articular derangement
Failure to respond, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The majority recover within a year with load management and rehabilitation, although symptoms can be prolonged; a minority with refractory disease may need shockwave therapy or, rarely, surgery.
pitfalls: Treating as inflammatory and relying on rest or repeated steroid injections rather than progressive loading
Corticosteroid injection giving short-term relief but poorer long-term outcomes
Missing radial tunnel syndrome, which can mimic or coexist
Overlooking the cervical spine as a source of referred pain
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: First-line management is load and activity modification, avoiding aggravating gripping and repetitive wrist extension while maintaining function
Refer for physiotherapy with a progressive, eccentric extensor-loading programme, the cornerstone of recovery
Provide symptomatic relief with topical or short-course oral NSAIDs and a counterforce forearm brace
Reserve corticosteroid injection for short-term relief only, recognising poorer long-term outcomes, and consider platelet-rich plasma in selected refractory cases
Offer extracorporeal shockwave therapy, and rarely surgical debridement of the extensor origin, for disease refractory to sustained conservative care
Reassure on the generally self-limiting natural history, and investigate atypical cases with nerve conduction studies to exclude radial tunnel syndrome
